candidate_sources.title: Alternaria triticina (leaf blight of wheat) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Alternaria triticina is a fungal plant pathogen responsible for the largest leaf blight issue in wheat. Infection causes small, oval, discolored lesions that enlarge to dark-brown or grey and irregular in shape, often with bright-yellow marginal zones. Infection requires hosts older than three weeks with symptoms appearing at 7-8 weeks. Conidia germinate at 20-25°C with 10 hours of water film on leaves. Management includes resistant cultivars, clean seed, chemical seed treatments, hot water treatments, and foliar fungicides (mancozeb, ziram, copper oxychloride, propineb).

candidate_sources.title: First Report of an Alternaria Leaf Spot of Wheat in the U.S.A.
candidate_sources.snippet: APS publication reporting the first documented occurrence of Alternaria leaf spot on wheat in the United States. Discusses identification of Alternaria spp. through pathogenicity assays and molecular sequencing methods, characterization of the pathogen, and implications for wheat disease management in North America.

candidate_sources.title: Alternaria triticina (leaf blight of wheat) | PlantWise Plus Knowledge Bank
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive resource on Alternaria triticina describing symptoms as small oval discolored lesions that become dark-brown to grey with irregular shape and bright-yellow marginal zones. Covers disease development requiring hosts older than 3 weeks with symptoms at 7-8 weeks. Details infection conditions (20-25°C, 10 hours water film or >90% humidity for 48 hours) and management strategies including resistant varieties, clean seed, chemical and hot water seed treatments, and foliar fungicides.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial leaf streak and black chaff on small grains
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial leaf streak (BLS) is a disease of wheat, barley, triticale, oats and many other cool- and warm-season grasses caused by Xanthomonas translucens. Infection characterized by irregular translucent water-soaked streaks on leaves that eventually turn yellow then brown. Advanced infections develop black chaff symptoms on glumes.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Leaf Streak and Black Chaff of Wheat | NDSU Agriculture
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial Leaf Streak and Black Chaff of Wheat caused by Xanthomonas translucens pv. undulosa. Symptoms include water-soaked lesions on leaves and dark purple to black streaks on glumes during grain fill. Disease is more prevalent with warm, humid weather conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Detection and Diagnosis of Bacterial Leaf Streak on Small Grain Cereals: From Laboratory to Field | Phytopathology®
candidate_sources.snippet: Peer-reviewed research on detection and diagnosis methods for Bacterial Leaf Streak caused by Xanthomonas translucens on wheat and other small grain cereals. Covers molecular and field-based diagnostic techniques for identifying the pathogen in laboratory and field conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat Disease Update: Bacterial Streak and Black Chaff
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Nebraska CropWatch article providing disease update on bacterial streak and black chaff in wheat, discussing symptom development, yield impacts ranging from negligible to over 50% loss, and disease management approaches.

candidate_sources.title: Barley yellow dwarf viruses (barley yellow dwarf) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: BYDVs are the most economically important virus disease of cereals and the most widespread. Barley yellow dwarf has been described as the most devastating cereal grain disease worldwide causing between 11% and 33% yield loss in wheat fields. Affected plants show yellowing or reddening of leaves, stunting, upright posture of thickened stiff leaves, reduced root growth, delayed heading, and yield reduction. Twenty-five aphids have been reported as vectors, with transmission restricted to Poaceae host range.

candidate_sources.title: Barley Yellow Dwarf of Wheat, Oats, and Barley | Ohioline
candidate_sources.snippet: Barley yellow dwarf symptoms include yellow, red, and/or purple discoloration of leaves from the tip down and from the margin to midrib. Infected plants may be stunted with decreased internode lengths. The disease is caused by at least eight viral species belonging to Luteoviridae family, transmitted by over 20 aphid species including Rhopalosiphum padi, R. maidis, Macrosiphum avenae, and Schizaphis graminum. This is the most widely distributed and economically important virus disease of wheat.

candidate_sources.title: Management suggestions for barley yellow dwarf virus control - Field Crops | Michigan State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Barley yellow dwarf virus (BYDV) causes between 11% and 33% yield loss in wheat. Management strategies include timely seeding in fall to avoid early aphid activity, controlling grassy weeds and volunteer cereals, planting resistant cultivars where available, and using insecticide seed treatments (imidacloprid, thiamethoxam, clothianidin) during the first 8-10 weeks after crop emergence to prevent aphid transmission. Symptoms include yellowing or reddening of leaves and stunting.

candidate_sources.title: Cephalosporium Stripe | Wheat & Small Grains | Washington State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Cephalosporium stripe is a vascular wilt disease of winter wheat and other small grains caused by the soilborne fungus Cephalosporium gramineum. Yellow (chlorotic) stripes in leaves of winter wheat are characteristic of this disease. A single leaf may have one to three stripes running from tip to base. The pathogen survives in infected crop residue and causes stunting and sterile seed heads.

candidate_sources.title: Cephalosporium Stripe | OSU Extension Service
candidate_sources.snippet: Cephalosporium stripe is caused by the fungus Cephalosporium gramineum. Symptoms include yellow stripes running from the tip of the leaf blade to its base and down the leaf sheath. Initially, stripes are yellow but develop brown (necrotic) stripes with age. The soilborne fungus overwinters in association with infected crop residue and is transmitted through root wounds.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat (Triticum aestivum)-Cephalosporium Stripe | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Cephalosporium stripe of wheat is caused by the soilborne fungus Cephalosporium gramineum. Longer breaks between susceptible crops reduces disease incidence because there is more time for colonized straw to decompose, reducing inoculum. Crop rotation of 2 years out of wheat is recommended for effective management of this vascular wilt disease.

candidate_sources.title: Tilletia tritici (wheat bunt) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet covering Identity, Overview, Distribution, Dispersal, Hosts/Species Affected, Diagnosis, Biology & Ecology, Seedborne Aspects, Natural Enemies, Impacts, Prevention/Control, and Further Information for Tilletia tritici, the causal agent of common bunt of wheat.

candidate_sources.title: Common Bunt of Wheat | Oklahoma State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Wheat grains are replaced by brown-black bunt balls containing dark spores with a distinctive fishy odor (trimethylamine). Heads may be off-green and appear greasy during flowering. Common bunt is favored by cool (<68°F), moist soil conditions, usually in fall-planted wheat. Fungicide seed treatments are effective management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Common bunt - UT Crops Pest Guides
candidate_sources.snippet: Bunt balls develop within the seed coat which becomes fragile and ruptures to reveal masses of black spores roughly the shape of a wheat kernel. Infected heads are thinner, do not lose green coloration as quickly, and symptoms appear during flowering. Caused by Tilletia caries and Tilletia laevis (synonymous with T. tritici and T. foetida).

candidate_sources.title: Common Bunt of Wheat 2010 | Kansas State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension factsheet documenting identification, symptom development, disease cycle, economic impact, and management recommendations including fungicide seed treatments for control of common bunt of wheat caused by Tilletia species.

candidate_sources.title: Tilletia laevis (smooth-spored wheat bunt) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet on Tilletia laevis, the smooth-spored wheat bunt pathogen. Covers identity, distribution, diagnosis, biology and ecology, seedborne aspects, impacts, and management strategies for this causal agent of common bunt of wheat.

candidate_sources.title: Dwarf Bunt of Wheat
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive encyclopedia entry on Dwarf Bunt disease, covering identification, pathogen biology (Tilletia controversa), symptoms including stunting and bunt balls, host specificity, and integrated disease management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Dwarf Bunt in Winter Wheat
candidate_sources.snippet: Utah State University extension publication on Dwarf Bunt affecting winter wheat, with detailed coverage of symptoms (yellow leaf flecking, stunting, excessive tillering, bunt balls with fishy odor), causal agent Tilletia controversa, environmental conditions favoring disease, and management including resistant varieties and fungicide options.

candidate_sources.title: Smuts and Bunts of Small Grains - Wheat
candidate_sources.snippet: Michigan State University extension guide covering smut and bunt diseases of wheat including Dwarf Bunt and Common Bunt, with symptoms, pathogen characteristics, disease cycle, conditions favoring infection, and chemical and cultural management recommendations.

candidate_sources.title: Eyespot of Wheat: How to identify and control this common fungal disease | OSU Extension Service
candidate_sources.snippet: Eyespot of wheat is a lower stem-infecting foot rot pathogen that limits winter wheat yields in the dryland Pacific Northwest. Eyespot infection results in characteristic elliptical or eye-shaped lesions on the lower stem with a dark brown perimeter and yellowish-brown center. Causal agents are Oculimacula yallundae and Oculimacula acuformis.

candidate_sources.title: Eyespot | Wheat & Small Grains | Washington State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Eyespot is a lower stem-infecting fungal disease caused by Oculimacula species that weakens stems through lesion development. The disease results in characteristic eye-shaped lesions on the lower stem portion with distinctive dark brown perimeters and yellowish centers containing pseudoparenchyma fruiting bodies.

candidate_sources.title: Eyespot of Wheat | Crop Protection Network
candidate_sources.snippet: Eyespot of wheat (also called strawbreaker foot rot) is caused by the fungi Oculimacula yallundae and Oculimacula acuformis. The disease is characterized by elliptical lesions on the lower stem that can cause lodging in severe infections. Management includes crop rotation, varietal resistance, and fungicide applications during the growing season.

candidate_sources.title: Common Root and Foot Rot of Wheat
candidate_sources.snippet: Symptoms include dark, chocolate brown to black lesions on the coleoptile, stem, roots, and/or subcrown internode. Heavily diseased roots result in stunting and poor tiller and root development. The pathogen that causes common root and foot rot is Bipolaris sorokiniana.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium Root, Crown, and Foot Rot of Wheat
candidate_sources.snippet: Symptoms include dark brown lesions on primary and secondary roots, and a dark brown to red lesion near the first node of the wheat plant. Pink, cottony fungal growth may be evident inside lower portions of infected stems. Fusarium crown rot is caused by Fusarium culmorum and F. pseudograminearum.

candidate_sources.title: Common Root Rot and Fusarium Foot Rot of Wheat (G1998)
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Nebraska–Lincoln extension publication detailing both common root rot caused by Bipolaris sorokiniana and Fusarium foot rot caused by Fusarium species, with comprehensive symptom descriptions, pathogen identification, and integrated management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Septoria Nodorum Blotch a.k.a. Septoria Glume Blotch
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Delaware Cooperative Extension factsheet on Septoria nodorum blotch, commonly known as glume blotch. Covers symptom identification on leaves and glumes, pathogen biology, and disease management strategies for wheat production.

candidate_sources.title: Stagonospora Glume Blotch
candidate_sources.snippet: Purdue Extension bulletin on Stagonospora glume blotch. Details symptoms including yellow spots on lower leaves that enlarge into gray or brown elliptical lesions, and characteristic pin-head black structures on glume surfaces. Covers the fungal pathogen Stagonospora nodorum and integrated management approaches.

candidate_sources.title: Glume Blotch in Wheat
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Kentucky IPM program resource on wheat glume blotch. Provides identification of symptoms on heads with gray/brown/purple lesions on the upper third of chaff, yield loss information (10-20% potential loss with shriveled grain), and management recommendations.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium Head Blight or Head Scab of Wheat, Barley and other Small Grain Crops | Ohioline
candidate_sources.snippet: Fusarium head blight (FHB) or head scab is caused by the fungus Fusarium graminearum. The earliest and most conspicuous symptom occurs soon after flowering, with diseased spikelets turning light-straw colored and having a bleached appearance. Pinkish to salmon-colored spore masses may form on the margin of the glumes within 7 to 10 days.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium Head Blight (Head Scab) of Wheat: Questions and Answers | Oklahoma State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Fusarium Head Blight (Head Scab) is a serious disease of wheat and other small grains caused by Fusarium graminearum. Infection occurs primarily during the flowering stage when wet, humid weather prevails. Two to three days of rainfall or extended periods of high relative humidity during flowering favor infection.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium Head Blight (Head Scab) - Purdue Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Fusarium Head Blight or Head Scab is one of the most important diseases of wheat. Typical scab symptoms include premature bleaching of the wheat head and shriveled, scabby kernels. The fungi causing scab produce mycotoxins, most notably vomitoxin (deoxynivalenol or DON), which may accumulate at high levels in harvested grain.

candidate_sources.title: Tilletia indica (Karnal bunt of wheat) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Karnal bunt of wheat is caused by the fungal pathogen Tilletia indica, a quarantine pest of high importance restricting global wheat trade. The disease invades kernels and replaces tissue with teliospores, producing a disagreeable fishy odor and causing yield and quality losses.

candidate_sources.title: Karnal Bunt | Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (USDA APHIS)
candidate_sources.snippet: Karnal bunt, caused by Tilletia indica, is a fungal disease affecting wheat, durum wheat, and triticale. Environmental conditions favoring disease include relative humidity over 70%, daytime temperatures of 18-24°C, and soil temperatures of 17-21°C. Management includes clean seed, sanitation, host resistance, and fungicide applications with 80% infection reduction using propiconazole.

candidate_sources.title: Extension Plant Pathology Loose Smut of Wheat
candidate_sources.snippet: Disease easily recognized at heading by characteristic dusty black appearance of diseased heads. Caused by fungus Ustilago tritici. Affected plants head out early, producing sterile heads with clumped, sooty olive-black spores in place of healthy glumes and kernels. Plant certified seed and use fungicide seed treatments for management.

candidate_sources.title: Loose smut of wheat - PLANT DISEASE - University of Illinois
candidate_sources.snippet: Loose smut (Ustilago tritici) infection colonizes developing embryos through wind-dispersed spores. Infected seeds carry dormant fungal mycelium that becomes active upon germination, growing systemically within the plant and reaching the developing seed head. Fungal mycelium replaces ovaries with masses of black spores.

candidate_sources.title: Loose Smut of Wheat
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive encyclopedia entry on loose smut disease of wheat with detailed information on symptoms, pathogen biology, and integrated management strategies including certified seed use and fungicide seed treatments.

candidate_sources.title: Powdery Mildew on Small Grains | Cooperative Extension | University of Delaware
candidate_sources.snippet: White cottony patches of mycelium and conidia on plant surface; yellow flecks visible on leaves; changes to grey-brown as plant matures. Caused by host-specific fungus.

candidate_sources.title: Powdery Mildew of Wheat - Nebraska Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Symptoms begin as small yellow flecks with white powdery growth; pathogen is Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici; favored by temperatures 50-70°F and high humidity without requiring free water.

candidate_sources.title: Identification and Control of Powdery Mildew of Wheat in Georgia | UGA Cooperative Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive guide covering identification of powdery mildew symptoms, pathogen biology, environmental conditions favoring infection, and management strategies for wheat production.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat (Triticum aestivum)-Pythium Root Rot | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Pythium spp. (syn. Globisporangium spp.) are fungus-like microorganisms that live for years in soil and on old root debris, parasitizing roots of wheat. Symptoms include reduced population and tillering, delayed maturation, stunted/chlorotic adult plants, and shriveled grain in severe infections.

candidate_sources.title: A review of wheat diseases—a field perspective
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive peer-reviewed review of wheat diseases including discussion of Pythium species as water molds (oomycetes) that move through water films and affect wheat seedlings and roots. Disease can be important in all wheat-producing areas.

candidate_sources.title: Two pathogenic species of Pythium: P. aphanidermatum and P. diclinum from a wheat field
candidate_sources.snippet: Peer-reviewed research documenting two pathogenic Pythium species (P. aphanidermatum and P. diclinum) isolated from wheat fields, providing molecular and morphological characterization of these wheat pathogens.

candidate_sources.title: Disease Caused by Pythium (Pythium) - Penn State
candidate_sources.snippet: University educational module providing detailed information on Pythium disease biology, symptoms, and management strategies for crops including wheat.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat Diseases Identification Pocket Guide - SDSU Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: South Dakota State University Extension guide for identifying and managing wheat diseases, including Pythium root rot with visual identification aids and management recommendations.

candidate_sources.title: Stripe Rust | Wheat & Small Grains | Washington State University
candidate_sources.snippet: On moderately resistant or resistant plants, the tissue in pustules often turns brown and dies, and fewer spores are produced. Varieties that are moderately resistant to the disease often will have more tan coloration to the lesion. Stripe rust can devastate wheat production, reducing yield by more than 70 percent in years when disease is severe.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat Stripe Rust
candidate_sources.snippet: Stripe rust symptoms first appear as small chlorotic lesions on leaves, with yellow to light orange pustules eventually emerging from these lesions. After tillering, pustules develop parallel to leaf veins, giving the foliage a distinct striped appearance. Moderately resistant varieties develop yellowish-white spots with a small amount of spore production in the center.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat Leaf Rust, Caused by Puccinia triticina, and Mitigation Through Host Genetic Resistance | Plant Health Cases
candidate_sources.snippet: The obligate fungal pathogen Puccinia triticina causes leaf rust symptoms on wheat worldwide. Different R genes influence the development of distinct resistance phenotypes. Genetic resistance is the primary control strategy, with over 80 known leaf rust resistance genes that are mostly race-specific and active from seedling stage to maturity.

candidate_sources.title: Disease Susceptibility of Wheat Varieties - Purdue Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Host reaction categories include resistant (R), moderately resistant (MR), moderately susceptible (MS), and susceptible (S). Resistance classifications for wheat diseases are standardized with these phenotype categories.

candidate_sources.title: Identification and Assessment of Resistance to Fusarium Head Blight and Mycotoxin Accumulation Among 99 Wheat Varieties
candidate_sources.snippet: Wheat cultivars evaluated for Fusarium head blight resistance with phenotypic classifications: R (resistant), MR (moderately resistant), MS (moderately susceptible), and S (susceptible). Assessment includes disease symptoms and mycotoxin accumulation levels.

candidate_sources.title: Effect of Quantitative Wheat Resistance on the Aggressiveness of Fusarium graminearum - Phytopathology
candidate_sources.snippet: Quantitative wheat resistance phenotypes to Fusarium graminearum measured across resistance spectrum from susceptible to resistant, with moderately susceptible phenotypes demonstrating intermediate disease development and pathogen aggressiveness.

candidate_sources.title: Important wheat diseases in the US and their management in the 21st century - Frontiers
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive review of important wheat diseases in the US covering causal organisms, economic damage, symptoms and host range, favorable conditions, and disease management strategies. Covers yellow rust, leaf rust, stem rust, powdery mildew, and Fusarium head blight with resistance phenotypes including race-specific and non-race specific resistance.

candidate_sources.title: Disease Resistance in Wheat - CABI Plant Protection Series
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive CABI Plant Protection reference work on disease resistance in wheat with 15 chapters focusing on the resistance of wheat to major diseases, covering genetic bases, resistance mechanisms, breeding strategies, and management approaches for economically important wheat diseases including leaf rust, stem rust, powdery mildew, and others.

candidate_sources.title: Major Foliar Fungal Diseases of Wheat in Oklahoma - Oklahoma State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension factsheet covering major foliar fungal diseases of wheat with identification, symptoms, and management recommendations including resistance gene selection and fungicide options.

candidate_sources.title: Disease Management in Wheat - UGA Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Georgia extension factsheet on integrated disease management in wheat. Covers host genetics, resistance breeding, chemical management strategies, and agronomic practices. Discusses role of resistant varieties and importance of not relying on fungicides alone. Includes guidance on variety selection for disease control.

candidate_sources.title: Disease Resistance in Wheat - CABI Plant Protection Series
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive CABI publication on disease resistance in wheat. Includes 15 chapters covering economically important wheat diseases, resistance mechanisms, breeding for resistance, pathogen variability, and recent advances in resistance genes. Specific chapters cover wheat powdery mildew resistance genes and morphological bases, wheat leaf rust resistance screening methods and biochemical bases.

candidate_sources.title: Controlling Root and Crown Diseases of Small Grain Cereals (PNW-639)
candidate_sources.snippet: Rhizoctonia solani causes damping-off, crown rot, and root rot in small grains. Symptoms include brick-red to black sunken lesions on coleoptiles and sub-crown internodes. Seedlings can be girdled and killed. Management includes seed treatment with fungicides, crop rotation, improved drainage, and avoiding cold wet soil conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Effects of damping-off caused by Rhizoctonia solani anastomosis group 2-1 on roots of wheat and oil seed rape quantified using X-ray Computed Tomography and real-time PCR
candidate_sources.snippet: This peer-reviewed study quantifies the effects of Rhizoctonia solani AG 2-1 damping-off on wheat roots using advanced imaging and molecular techniques. Recent soil surveys in USA and UK show R. solani AG2-1 present in >69% of fields. Wheat exhibits fewer symptoms and develops more complex root systems compared to oilseed rape. Study details host-pathogen interactions including root necrosis, cortex tissue maceration, and stunting.

candidate_sources.title: Small Grain Root and Crown Diseases
candidate_sources.snippet: Montana State University Extension guide covering root and crown diseases of wheat, barley, and other small grains caused by Rhizoctonia solani and other pathogens. Discusses damping-off symptoms, disease cycle, factors favoring infection, and integrated management strategies including seed treatment, proper seedbed preparation, crop rotation, and cultural practices.

candidate_sources.title: Leaf Blotch Diseases of Wheat—Septoria tritici Blotch, Stagonospora nodorum Blotch and Tan Spot
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension factsheet covering Septoria tritici blotch with symptoms (irregular brown lesions restricted by leaf veins), pathogen identification (Zymoseptoria tritici), and integrated disease management strategies including crop rotation and varietal resistance.

candidate_sources.title: Septoria Tritici Blotch
candidate_sources.snippet: Kansas State University Department of Plant Pathology extension document dedicated to Septoria tritici blotch. Covers disease symptoms (elongated lesions with pycnidia), pathogen biology (Zymoseptoria tritici, formerly Septoria tritici), and management recommendations.

candidate_sources.title: Fungal Leaf Spot Diseases of Wheat: Tan spot, Septoria/Stagonospora nodorum blotch and Septoria tritici blotch
candidate_sources.snippet: NDSU Agriculture extension guide providing comprehensive information on Septoria tritici blotch symptoms, disease cycle, and integrated pest management strategies for wheat producers.

candidate_sources.title: Sharp eyespot symptoms in cereals | AHDB
candidate_sources.snippet: Authoritative UK source specifically dedicated to sharp eyespot symptoms in cereals. Describes sharply defined lesions on leaf sheaths with dark brown borders and characteristic holes in centers. Caused by Rhizoctonia cerealis. Covers environmental conditions favoring disease (cool temperatures, acidic soils).

candidate_sources.title: Rust Diseases of Wheat
candidate_sources.snippet: Stem rust pustules are large, orange-red, oval to elongated, and develop predominantly on the stem, leaf blade and sheath. The uredinia tear the plant tissue, giving the affected stem and leaf a distinctly tattered appearance. Caused by Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat Stem Rust - Cereal Disease Lab
candidate_sources.snippet: Stem rust is favored by hot days 25-30°C, mild nights 15-20°C with adequate moisture. Losses are often severe (50 to 70%) over a large area and individual fields can be totally destroyed. Damage is greatest when disease becomes severe before grain is completely formed.

candidate_sources.title: Rust Diseases of Wheat - Nebraska Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive guide to wheat rust diseases including stem rust identification, epidemiology, and management practices. Covers disease development under environmental conditions and integrated pest management strategies for wheat producers.

candidate_sources.title: Leaf, Stem, and Stripe Rust Diseases of Wheat
candidate_sources.snippet: New Mexico State University extension publication providing detailed information on stem rust symptoms, disease cycle, and management recommendations for wheat growers in the Southwest region.

candidate_sources.title: Stripe Rust (Yellow Rust) of Wheat | CAES Field Report
candidate_sources.snippet: Stripe Rust, also known as Yellow Rust, is a serious disease of wheat caused by Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici. Under favorable cool and moist conditions, the disease can devastate wheat production. Symptoms include chlorotic lesions and yellow to light orange pustules (uredia) arranged in linear stripes on leaves. Host plant resistance is the most effective control method.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat stripe rust - USDA ARS Cereal Disease Lab
candidate_sources.snippet: Wheat stripe rust is the major rust disease affecting winter cereal production worldwide. Uredospores are wind-dispersed over long distances, with most inoculum for wheat produced in northern regions originating from long-distance spore movement. The disease is difficult to culture on artificial media and reduces yield by more than 70% in severe years under favorable conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat Take-All Root Rot - Kansas State University Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Life Cycle The fungus that causes take-all root rot survives... Diseased plants are easy to pull from the soil since the roots are short and few in number. Plants affected by Take-all have darkened stem bases and black, brittle roots.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat Take-All - MU Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Take-all is caused by the fungus Gaeumannomyces graminis. It infects wheat, barley, rye and several grasses. Rotate crops so a field is out of wheat for one to three years and in a crop that is not infected, such as corn, forage legumes, milo, oats, or soybean.

candidate_sources.title: Take-All Disease Fact Sheet - Soil Quality Australia
candidate_sources.snippet: Take-all is a common worldwide root disease of wheat caused by the soil-borne fungus Gaeumannomyces graminis var tritici. Practices including crop rotation with non-host crops, canola (Brassica napus), applying balanced ammonium fertilizer, and delayed seeding help control the disease.

candidate_sources.title: Tan Spot of Wheat
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Nebraska-Lincoln extension publication dedicated to tan spot of wheat. Covers pathogen (Pyrenophora tritici-repentis), symptom development from lower leaves upward, and management recommendations including resistant varieties and crop rotation strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Tan spot of cereals
candidate_sources.snippet: APS (American Phytopathological Society) educational resource on tan spot of cereals. Provides information on disease symptoms, pathogen biology, disease cycle, and management approaches for wheat and other cereal crops.

candidate_sources.title: Barley Yellow Dwarf Virus | Cooperative Extension | University of Delaware
candidate_sources.snippet: Barley yellow dwarf virus affects wheat, oats, and barley. Transmitted by aphid vectors including oat bird-cherry aphid, corn leaf aphid, English grain aphid, and greenbug. Causes yellowing and dwarfing of affected plants with significant yield impacts.

candidate_sources.title: Barley Yellow Dwarf | CropWatch | Nebraska
candidate_sources.snippet: Barley yellow dwarf is the most widely distributed and economically most important virus disease of wheat. Symptoms include leaf discoloration in shades of yellow, red, or purple. Multiple viral species in Luteoviridae family cause the disease through aphid transmission.

candidate_sources.title: Hymenula cerealis (Cephalosporium stripe) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive datasheet covering Hymenula cerealis (sexual stage of Cephalosporium gramineum), the causal agent of Cephalosporium stripe in wheat. Includes identity, overview, distribution, biology, ecology, and control measures for this vascular wilt disease of winter wheat and cereal crops.

candidate_sources.title: Puccinia triticina (wheat brown rust)
candidate_sources.snippet: Leaf rust, caused by Puccinia triticina, is the most common rust disease of wheat. The pathogen infects leaves, causing orange to red pustules, containing millions of urediniospores, reducing the photosynthetic area and causing desiccation and yield loss.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat Leaf Rust
candidate_sources.snippet: Leaf rust, also known as brown rust, is caused by the fungus Puccinia triticina. The wheat rust fungi are obligate parasites; that is, they can grow and multiply in nature only on living plant tissue and are highly specialized in the plant species they parasitize.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat Streak Mosaic Virus | CropWatch | Nebraska
candidate_sources.snippet: Wheat streak mosaic (WSM), caused by Wheat Streak Mosaic Virus (WSMV), is a common disease in many wheat growing regions. Leaves of infected plants show a yellowed mosaic pattern of parallel discontinuous streaks. WSMV is transmitted by the wheat curl mite (Aceria tosichella) and threatens wheat production worldwide.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat Streak Mosaic Virus
candidate_sources.snippet: Wheat streak mosaic virus (WSMV) is a plant pathogenic virus of the family Potyviridae that infects plants in the family Poaceae, especially wheat. It is globally distributed and vectored by the wheat curl mite. Symptoms include light green to yellow mottled mosaic with stunting and reduced tillering. Yield losses up to 100% have been reported.

candidate_sources.title: Wheat Streak Mosaic Virus Showing Up in Fields
candidate_sources.snippet: Wheat streak mosaic disease is developing in winter wheat fields. Infected plants display yellowed mosaic patterns and are typically stunted and splayed on the ground. WSMV shows synergistic interactions with other viruses (Triticum mosaic virus and High plains virus), further exacerbating crop yield problems.
